topic.title: Symmetry, Equivariance, and Canonical Representations
topic.overview: Symmetry-aware learning makes outputs transform predictably when inputs rotate, translate, or undergo another structured change. Some methods constrain the architecture; others first map inputs into a learned canonical frame. The appropriate choice depends on whether a transformation should preserve the answer or change it in a known way.
topic.whyItMatters: Encoding a valid symmetry can reduce redundant learning, but enforcing the wrong one can remove useful information. Canonicalization also introduces its own ambiguity when several orientations or configurations are equally plausible.
topic.evolution: The representatives span constrained higher-order networks in 1987, learned invariants, and later group-based geometric models. Recent work combines learned canonicalization, approximate equivariance, and applications such as rotation-invariant spherical watermarking. These examples broaden the transformations and data spaces considered while retaining the need to specify the group action precisely.
openQuestions: How should models handle ambiguous canonical frames without unstable predictions?
When is approximate symmetry more useful than an exact architectural constraint?
